items.t: Tŷ Mawr: the Great House of Llandough
items.d: The historic environment record lists Tŷ Mawr, beside the church of St Dochdwy, as the principal freehold of the parish, with details pointing to the seventeenth century.

items.t: 1824: the first record that names the house
items.d: The earliest record found that names Tŷ Mawr is David Stewart’s survey of 1824. The family dates its arrival at the house to 1667.

items.t: 1974: “an ancient Welsh house” and 1,700 names
items.d: In April 1974 the national press reported an open day to save “an ancient Welsh house”, Tŷ Mawr, Llandough. Local history records 1,700 signatures on a petition that year…

items.t: What the courts decided, and what the record leaves open
items.d: The High Court in 1986 and the Court of Appeal in 1987 decided possession and limitation. Paper title was not in issue.

items.t: 46 records that should exist
items.d: The missing records register lists 46 records that should exist. None is in the archive, and 19 were searched for and not found.

items.t: 1000 Cuts: a dated chronology, 1870s to 1988
items.d: A dated chronology of the Williams family’s position at Great House Farm in law and in fact, each step linked to its evidence.

items.t: The Wayback Vault: dated copies of the web
items.d: Dated static copies of web pages that concern Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, grouped by site, with images, documents, video and text.

items.t: Cydwin, Cedwyn, Ty Mawr: every name the records use
items.d: Great House Farm appears in the records under 26 different wordings, and Llandough under nine.

items.t: Lavernock Point, 11 May 1897
items.d: From the cliff at Lavernock the first wireless messages crossed open sea, to Flat Holm and a week later to Brean Down. The guided tour stops there.
